<div sID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Zeph.2" sID="Zeph.2"/> <div eID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20662" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. An earnest exhortation to the nation of the Jews to repent and make their peace with God, and so to prevent the judgments threatened before it was too late (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), and this inferred from the revelation of God's wrath against them in the foregoing chapter. II. A denunciation of the judgments of God against several of the neighbouring nations that had assisted, or rejoiced in, the calamity of Israel. 1. The Philistines, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.4-Zeph.2.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. The Moabites and Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8-Zeph.2.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 3. The Ethiopians and Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.12-Zeph.2.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. All these shall drink of the same cup of trembling that is put into the hands of God's people, as was also foretold by other prophets before and after.

(<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired; <hi type="super">2</hi> Before the decree bring forth, <hi type="italic">before</hi> the day pass as the chaff, before the fierce anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> come upon you, before the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anger come upon you. <hi type="super">3</hi> Seek ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anger. <div eID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> Here we see what the prophet meant in that terrible description of the approaching judgments which we had in the foregoing chapter. From first to last his design was, not to drive the people to despair, but to drive them to God and to their duty—not to frighten them out of their wits, but to frighten them out of their sins. In pursuance of that he here calls them to repentance, national repentance, as the only way to prevent national ruin. Observe, <div eID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> I. The summons given them to a national assembly (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gather yourselves together.</hi> He had told them, in the last words of the foregoing chapter, that God would make a <hi type="italic">speedy riddance of all that dwelt in the land,</hi> upon which, one would think, it should follow, "Disperse yourselves, and flee for shelter where you can find a place." When the decree had absolutely gone forth for the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, that was the advice given (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Matt. xxiv. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Then let those who are in Judea flee into the mountains;</hi> but here it is otherwise. God warns, that he may not wound, threatens, that he may not strike, and therefore calls to the people to use means for the turning away of his wrath. The summons is given to a <hi type="italic">nation not desired.</hi> The word signifies either, 1. <hi type="italic">Not desiring,</hi> that has not any desires towards God or the remembrance of his name, is not desirous of his favour or grace, but very indifferent to it, has no mind to repent and reform. "Yet <hi type="italic">come together,</hi> and see if you can stir up desires in one another." Thus God is often <hi type="italic">found of those that sought him not,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">asked for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa. lxv. 1</reference>. Or, 2. <hi type="italic">Not desirable,</hi> no ways lovely, nor having any thing in them amiable, or which might recommend them to God. The land of Israel had been a <hi type="italic">pleasant land, a land of delight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Dan. xi. 41</reference>); but now it is unlovely, it is a <hi type="italic">nation not desired,</hi> to which God might justly say, <hi type="italic">Depart from me;</hi> but he says, "<hi type="italic">Gather together to me,</hi> and let us see if any expedient can be found out for the preventing of the ruin. <hi type="italic">Gather together,</hi> that you may in a body humble yourselves before God, may fast, and pray, and seek his face. <hi type="italic">Gather together,</hi> to consult among yourselves what is to be done in this critical juncture, that every one may consider of it, may give and take advice, and speak his mind, and that what is done may be done by consent and so may be a national act." Some read it, "<hi type="italic">Enquire into yourselves,</hi> yea, <hi type="italic">enquire into yourselves;</hi> examine your consciences; look into your hearts; search and try your ways; <hi type="italic">enquire into yourselves,</hi> that you may find out the sin by which God has been provoked to this displeasure against you, and may find out the way of returning to him." Note, When God is contending with us it concerns us to enquire into ourselves. <div eID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> II. Arguments urged to press them to the utmost seriousness and expedition herein (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.2">v. 2</reference>): "Do it in earnest; do it with all speed before it is too late, <hi type="italic">before the decree bring forth, before the day pass.</hi>" The manner of speaking here is very lively and awakening, designed to make them apprehensive, as all sinners are concerned to be, 1. That their danger is very great, that their all lies at stake, that it is a matter of life and death, which therefore well requires and well deserves the closest application of mind that can be. It is not a trifle, and therefore is not a thing to be trifled about. It is the <hi type="italic">fierce anger of the Lord</hi> that is kindled against them, and is just ready to kindle upon them, that <hi type="italic">devouring fire</hi> which none can <hi type="italic">dwell with,</hi> which none can make head against or hold up their head under. "It is the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord's anger,</hi> the day set for the pouring out of the full vials of it, that you are threatened with, that <hi type="italic">great day of the Lord</hi>" spoken of, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.14">ch. i. 14</reference>. "Are you not concerned to prepare for that day?" 2. That it is very imminent: "Bestir yourselves now quickly, <hi type="italic">before the decree bring forth,</hi> and then it will be too late, the opportunity will be lost and never retrieved. The decree is as it were big with child, and it will <hi type="italic">bring forth the day,</hi> the terrible day, which shall <hi type="italic">pass as chaff,</hi> which shall hurry you away into captivity as chaff before the wind." <hi type="italic">We know not what a day may bring forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Prov. xxvii. 1</reference>), but we do know what the decree will bring forth against impenitent sinners, whom therefore it highly concerns to repent in time, in <hi type="italic">the accepted time.</hi> Note, It is the wisdom of those whom God has a controversy with to agree with him quickly, while they are in the way, before his fierce anger comes upon them, not to be turned away. In a case of this nature delays are highly dangerous and may be fatal; they will be so if by them the heart is hardened. They must <hi type="italic">seek the Lord,</hi> seek his favour and grace, address him upon all occasions, ask of him what they need, seek him early, seek him diligently, and continue seeking him. It is the distinguishing character of the people of God that they are the meek ones of the earth; this is their badge; it is their livery. They are modest, and humble, and low in their own eyes; they are mild, and gentle, and yielding to others, not soon angry, not very angry, not long angry; they are the quiet in the land, Ps. xxxv. 20 . And they are subject and submissive to their God, to all his precepts and all his providences. Actuated by this principle and disposition, they have wrought his judgments, that is, have obeyed his laws, observed his institutions, have made conscience of their duty to him, and have laid out themselves for the advancement of his honour and interest in the world. 2. What they are required to do; they must seek, which denotes both a careful enquiry and a constant endeavour, that they may know and do their duty. (1.) They must seek the Lord, seek his favour and grace, address him upon all occasions, ask of him what they need, seek him early, seek him diligently, and continue seeking him. (2.) They must seek righteousness. "Seek to God for the performance of his promises to you, and see to it that you abound yet more in duty to him; seek for the righteousness of Christ to be imputed to you, for the graces of God's Spirit to be implanted in you; hunger and thirst after them." (3.) They must seek meekness. This is a grace they were so eminent for that they were denominated the meek of the land, and yet this they must seek. Note, Those that are ever so good must still strive to be better, those that have ever so much grace must be still praying and labouring for more. Nay, those that excel in any particular grace must still seek to excel yet more in that, because in that most assaults will be made upon them by their enemies, in that most is expected from them by their friends, and in that they are most apt to be themselves secure. Si dixisti, Sufficit, periisti—Say but, I am all that I ought to be, and you are undone. In the difficult trying times approaching, the meek will find exercise for all the meekness they have, and all little enough, and therefore should seek it earnestly, and pray that when God in his providence gives them occasion for it he would by his grace enable them to exercise it, to show all meekness to all men, in all instances, that, as the day is, so may the strength be. Though the day of the Lord's anger do come upon the land, yet you shall be safe, you shall be taken under special protection. Verily it shall be well with thy remnant, Jer. xv. 11 . Thy life will I give unto thee for a prey, Jer. xlv. 5 . I will deliver thee in that day, Jer. xxxix. 17 . It may be, you shall be hid; if any be hid, you shall." Good men cannot be sure of temporal preservation, for all things come alike to all, but they are most likely to be hid, and stand fairest for a distinguishing care of Providence. It is expressed thus doubtfully to try if they will trust the goodness of God's nature, though they have but the it may be of a promise, and to keep up in them a holy fear and watchfulness lest they should seem to come short, and should do any thing to throw themselves out of the divine protection. Note, those that hold fast their integrity, in times of common iniquity, have reason to hope that God will find out a hiding-place for them, where they shall be safe and easy, in times of common calamity. They shall be hid (as Luther says) aut in cœlo, aut sub cœlo—either in heaven or under heaven, either in the possession of heaven or under the protection of heaven. Or, 2. "You of this nation, though it be a nation not desired, yet, in the day of the Lord's anger with the neighbouring nations, when his judgments are abroad, you shall be hid; your land shall be preserved for the sake of those few meek ones that stand in the gap to turn away the wrath of God. If we prepare an ark, that shall be our hiding-place, Gen. vii. 1 .

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen20673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Punishment of Various Nations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> against their border. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the breeding of nettles, and salt-pits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. <hi type="super">10</hi> This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> against the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">will be</hi> terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall worship him, every one from his place, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the isles of the heathen. <div eID="gen20674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20675" type="x-p"/> The Moabites and Ammonites were both of the posterity of Lot; their countries joined, and, both adjoining to Israel, they are here put together in the prophecy against them. <div eID="gen20675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20676" type="x-p"/> I. They are both charged with the same crime, and that was reproaching and reviling the people of God and triumphing in their calamities (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have reproached my people;</hi> while God's people kept close to their duty it is probable that they reproached them for the singularities of their religion; and now that they had revolted from God, and fallen under his displeasure, they reproached them for that too. It has been the common lot of God's people in all ages to be reproached and reviled upon one account or other. Thus the old serpent spits his venom; and pride is at the bottom of it; it is in their pride that they have <hi type="italic">magnified themselves against the people of the Lord of hosts,</hi> thinking themselves as good as they, as great, and every way as happy. It is the <hi type="italic">comtempt of the proud</hi> that God's people are filled with, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>. They have <hi type="italic">spoken big</hi> (so some read it, <hi type="italic">magna locuti sunt—they have spoken great things) against their border</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">v. 8</reference>), against those of them that bordered upon their country, whom upon all occasions they insulted, or against the property they claimed, which they disputed, or the protection they boasted of, which they ridiculed; they <hi type="italic">spoke big against the people of the Lord of hosts</hi> as a deserted abandoned people. <hi type="italic">Great swelling words of vanity</hi> are the genuine language of the church's enemies. "But <hi type="italic">I have heard them</hi>" (says God), "and will let you know that I have heard them. I have heard, and I will reckon for them," <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. And, if God hears the reproaches and revilings we are under, it is a good reason why we should be as a <hi type="italic">deaf man that hears not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14-Ps.38.15">Ps. xxxviii. 14, 15</reference>. Nay, God not only takes notice of, but interests himself in the reproaches cast on his people, because they are his; and it is certain that those who look with disdain upon the people of the Lord of hosts thereby dishonour the Lord of hosts himself. See this very thing charged on Moab and Ammon, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">Ezek. xxv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen20676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20677" type="x-p"/> II. They are both laid under the same doom. Associates in iniquity may expect to be such in desolation. See with what solemnity sentence is pronounced upon them, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.9">v. 9</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> the sovereign Lord of all, who has authority to pass this sentence and ability to execute it; it is <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> who is jealous for their honour; it is he that has said it, nay, he has sworn it, <hi type="italic">As I live, saith the Lord.</hi> The sentence is, 1. That the Moabites and Ammonites shall be quite destroyed; they <hi type="italic">shall be as Sodom and Gomorrah,</hi> the marks of whose ruins in the Dead Sea lay near adjoining to the countries of Moab and Ammon; they shall, though not by the same means (even fire from heaven), Yet almost in the same manner, be laid waste; not again to be inhabited, or not of a long time. The country shall produce nothing but <hi type="italic">nettles,</hi> instead of corn; and there shall be <hi type="italic">brine-pits,</hi> instead of the pleasant fountains of water with which the country had abounded. 2. That Israel shall be too hard for them, shall <hi type="italic">spoil them</hi> of their goods and <hi type="italic">possess</hi> their country by lawful war. Note, Proud men sometimes, by the just judgment of God, fall under the mortification of being trampled upon themselves by those whom once they haughtily trampled upon. And <hi type="italic">this shall they have for their pride.</hi> <div eID="gen20677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20678" type="x-p"/> III. Other nations shall in like manner be humbled, that the Lord alone may be exalted (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will be terrible</hi> unto the Moabites and Ammonites in particular, who have made themselves a terror to his Israel. For, 1. Heathen gods must be abolished. They have long had possession, and their worshippers have both glorified them and gloried in them. But <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> will <hi type="italic">famish all the gods of the earth,</hi> will starve them out of their strong-holds.
